sources.title: Human History Map historical-basemap civilization index
sources.note: Exact repository record checked: scythians-bc200 is a circa culture record dated 200 BCE to 200 CE and is distinct from other Scythian, Saka, Sarmatian and Alan ids.

sources.title: Human History Map world-300 BCE topology
sources.note: Decoded predecessor seam. The exact scythians-bc200 id is absent, so its later first appearance is an atlas change rather than a documented founding event.

sources.title: Human History Map world-200 BCE topology
sources.note: Decoded exact identity: three separate features share the id, Bactria, Bosporan Kingdom and an unlabeled three-part umbrella, with independently hashed coordinates and strongly discontinuous footprints.

sources.title: Human History Map world-100 BCE topology
sources.note: Decoded exact successor: one three-part MultiPolygon, four rings and 328 positions across Central Asia, not a continuation of every 200 BCE component.

sources.title: Human History Map world-1 BCE topology
sources.note: Decoded coverage gap. The exact id is absent at the 1 BCE snapshot even though historically documented communities continued in several regions.

sources.title: Human History Map world-100 CE topology
sources.note: Decoded exact late feature: one 79-position Polygon around Crimea and the lower Don, far west of the preceding Central Asian footprint.

sources.title: Human History Map world-200 CE topology
sources.note: Decoded ending seam. The exact id is absent at the 200 CE snapshot, which records the end of imported coverage rather than extinction.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Scythians
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis used for the overview: terminology, the Crimean kingdom, Hellenization, settlements, political change and survival through mixed later communities.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Sakas in Afghanistan
sources.note: Scholarly review of Saka and Yuezhi movements, the contested attribution of Bactrian finds, Sakastan and evidence from coins rather than a single migration narrative.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Indo-Scythian Dynasty
sources.note: Dynastic chronology and evidence for Indo-Scythian rulers from the late second century BCE into the first century CE, including acknowledged chronological uncertainty.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Scythian Language
sources.note: Linguistic assessment explaining that Scythian is known mainly through names, glosses and indirect evidence rather than securely preserved continuous native texts.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Afghanistan, Hidden Treasures
sources.note: Museum synthesis of Bactria and Tillya Tepe, including six first-century tombs, portable gold, long-distance materials and uncertainty over the buried group’s identity.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Afghanistan exhibition photo gallery
sources.note: Object-level record for the collapsible gold crown and other Tillya Tepe ornaments, including measurements, materials, tomb context and portable construction.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Year One
sources.note: Metropolitan Museum catalogue used to place the six princely Tillya Tepe burials and their mixed artistic traditions in the first century CE.

sources.title: Ashmolean Heberden Coin Room: Indo-Scythian coin of Azes
sources.note: Museum object record for an Azes coin around 48 to 25 BCE with Greek and Kharoshthi-Gandhari royal legends and a mounted ruler.

sources.title: Ashmolean Heberden Coin Room: coin of Azilises
sources.note: Object record for a copper Indo-Scythian coin with Greek and Kharoshthi legends, an elephant and a humped bull.

sources.title: British Museum: coin of Azes II
sources.note: Museum object record for a bilingual Indo-Scythian coin found at the Bimaran stupa complex, with mounted king and Greek and Kharoshthi inscriptions.

sources.title: Searchable Greek Inscriptions: Decree for Diophantos
sources.note: Digital scholarly edition of the Chersonesan Greek decree naming Palakos, Scythians and Diophantos during the wars around 110 to 107 BCE.

sources.title: IRIS Greek Coinage: Olbia results
sources.note: Scholarly coin database records issues of Skilurus at Olbia and their civic, divine, agricultural and military imagery.

sources.title: Scythian Neapolis Historical and Archaeological Museum-Reserve
sources.note: Site museum account of the fortified capital, houses, granary, mausoleum, Greek inscriptions, wine complex and archaeological discoveries.

sources.title: Chersonesos Taurica Museum: ancient history
sources.note: Site museum history used for Diophantos’s campaigns and the Roman intervention that relieved a Scythian siege in the 60s CE.

sources.title: Chersonesos Taurica Museum: Ust-Alma
sources.note: Museum account of the large Late Scythian settlement and necropolis at Ust-Alma on Crimea’s western coast.

sources.title: Russian Archaeology: Early Crypts of the Ust-Alma Burial Ground
sources.note: Peer-reviewed archaeological abstract documenting early crypt construction, multiple chambers and dated assemblages including pottery, brooches, buckles, bracelets and beads.

sources.title: Ancient Civilizations from Scythia to Siberia: A Warrior Burial from Ust-Alma
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study of a mid-first-century CE elite warrior burial with weapons, clothing ornaments, vessels and imported goods.

sources.title: Arts: Children in the Late Scythian Funerary Record
sources.note: Peer-reviewed analysis of child dress and burial display, stressing symbolism, social expectation and the limits of assigning ethnicity from objects.

sources.title: Terra Sigillata from the Late Scythian Fortress Alma Kermen
sources.note: University repository record for a specialist study of roughly 350 terra-sigillata vessels and associated beads, rings and grooming containers.

sources.title: Dental Pathologies of the Late Scythians from Chervony Mayak
sources.note: Peer-reviewed dental study of 106 individuals, relating calculus, caries and tooth wear cautiously to protein, carbohydrates, age and social differences.

sources.title: Antiquity: Mysterious red cinnabar from Chervony Mayak
sources.note: Peer-reviewed report of cinnabar in two female burials, with pigment, cosmetic and funerary interpretations presented as alternatives rather than established medicine.

sources.title: PLOS ONE: Isotopes and mobility in the Scythian era
sources.note: Open peer-reviewed study of human diet and mobility through 700 to 200 BCE, showing varied local lives and millet consumption near this card’s opening.

sources.title: UNESCO Silk Roads: Almaty
sources.note: UNESCO regional synthesis describing Saka-period farming, cattle breeding, burial mounds and material remains north of the Tianshan.

sources.title: German Archaeological Institute: Jewelry from Chervony Mayak burial 128
sources.note: Archaeological institute account of gold garment plaques from a woman’s burial and the loss of context caused by looting and war.

sources.title: Journal of Ancient History and Archaeology: Chervony Mayak necropolis
sources.note: Peer-reviewed site overview for a Late Scythian hillfort and burial ground on the lower Dnieper, including research and preservation context.

proposedOverrides.summary: An atlas umbrella links Saka and Late Scythian worlds across Asia and Crimea; changing kingdoms, settlements and mixed traditions continued beyond its map cutoff.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact id scythians-bc200 is indexed circa 200 BCE to 200 CE and had no tracked card or override before integration.

At 200 BCE the id occurs three times: a 53-position Bactria Polygon, a 64-position two-part Bosporan Kingdom MultiPolygon, and a 519-position three-part unlabeled MultiPolygon. Each coordinate array has a separate audited SHA-256.

At 100 BCE it becomes one 328-position, three-part Central Asian MultiPolygon. It is absent at 1 BCE, then returns at 100 CE as one 79-position Crimean/lower-Don Polygon. These discontinuities are atlas categorization, not literal mobile borders.
The separate scythians, proto-scythian-culture, saka-kingdom, sarmates, sarmatians and alans ids remain distinct. No appliesTo alias or shared-card substitution is used.
Every point test and coordinate bound describes imported display geometry only. It cannot establish political control, ethnicity, language, migration or modern territorial claims.
